new_statements.quote: Although a few words are distinguished by high vs. low tone, Fa d’Ambô seems to no longer be a tone language. The accent normally falls on the penultimate syllable and except for these few words no tone differentiation is made.
new_statements.citation: Post, Marike. 2013. Fa d'Ambô. In Susanne Maria Michaelis, Philippe Maurer, Martin Haspelmath & Magnus Huber (eds.), The survey of pidgin and creole languages, vol. 2: Portuguese-based, Spanish-based, and French-based languages, 81-89. Oxford: Oxford University Press. Read as APiCS Online survey chapter 38 (https://apics-online.info/surveys/38).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (and the dump, lines 180-182). The §4 Phonology passage is present verbatim in the HTML: "Although a few words are distinguished by high vs. low tone, Fa d'Ambô seems to no longer be a tone language. The accent normally falls on the penultimate syllable and except for these few words no tone differentiation is made." (the dump only adds a stray space before the comma where the markup was stripped). Contributor is shown as Marike Post (apics-online.info/contributors/postmarike); the chapter is APiCS contribution 38 "Fa d'Ambô", introduced as "the language of the island of Annobón.. Gulf of Guinea", speakers on Annobón and in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea — i.e. Glottolog fada12…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent normally falls on the penultimate syllable; a residual lexical high/low tone contrast survives on a handful of words only, and long-vowel syllables carry a rising (LH) pitch whether or not they are stressed. The older primary description (Vila 1891, 'Prosodia', saved) refines this in a Portuguese-like way: vowel-final words of two or three syllables are penult-stressed, but verbs (and many adverbs) are always oxytone and consonant-final words are oxytone; the stress-marked transcriptions in Silveira et al. 2013 (pp. 31-32) match Vila ([ˈgula], [ˈbu:du] vs. verbs [lɛ:ˈva], [xõˈta], [mu:ˈta] and [xaˈsol] 'dog'). So 'penult' is the default for vowel-final non-verbs, with a lexical-class/final-consonant conditioned final-stress pattern.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Post: 'a few words' distinguished by high vs low tone; long-vowel syllables always rising tone regardless of stress. Vila 1891: verbs and many adverbs oxytone (amoyá, amapassá, danjí); consonant-final words oxytone (vigil, tambol). Silveira et al. 2013 (pp. 40-41): in yes/no questions stress may shift to the last mora of the final word ('acentue a última mora.. mesmo se a palavra não possuir acento final') together with rising intonation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms) in Post and Vila; the interrogative stress shift in Silveira et al. 2013 is a phrase-final/intonational process. Fa d'Ambô is described as a residually tonal language (APiCS feature 120: simple lexical tone system), so 'accent' here is stress-like prominence coexisting with marginal lexical tone.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Fa d'Ambô proper (fada1250) as spoken on Annobón (and by the Malabo diaspora); Post's APiCS chapter documents the Annobón lect. Vila 1891 calls it 'Ambú'; Schuchardt 1888 'Negerportugiesisch von Annobom'. No dialect split relevant to stress is reported.

new_statements.quote: p. 312: "Em santome, fa d'ambô, lung'i e angolar, o acento pode ser atribuído à última, penúltima ou antepenúltima sílaba como em (2): ... Fa d'ambô final [bO"nE] 'boina' prefinal ["pÕte] 'ponte' antepenúltimo ["pulusu] 'pulso'". p. 314: "caso o item nominal termine com um molde silábico CV — sílaba leve, isto é, monomoraica—, o acento é atribuído à penúltima sílaba ... se a palavra terminar com uma sílaba CVC — sílaba pesada, isto é, bimoraica—, ao pé, formado com duas moras, lhe será atribuído o acento. Quanto aos verbos, ao constatar que todas as línguas-filhas apresentavam um padrão acentual idêntico, os verbos foram reconstruídos com acento na última sílaba" (ex. (4) [ka"ma] (FA) 'queimar').
new_statements.translation: p. 312: "In Santome, Fa d'Ambô, Lung'ie and Angolar, the accent can be assigned to the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, as in (2): ... Fa d'Ambô: final [bO'nE] 'beret', prefinal ['pÕte] 'bridge', antepenultimate ['pulusu] 'wrist'." p. 314: "if the nominal item ends in a CV template - a light, i.e. monomoraic, syllable - the accent is assigned to the penultimate syllable ... if the word ends in a CVC syllable - heavy, i.e. bimoraic - the foot formed by its two moras receives the accent. As for verbs, having found that all the daughter languages showed an identical accentual pattern, verbs were reconstructed with accent on the final syllable" (e.g. [ka'ma] (FA) 'to burn').

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with Post 2013's 'accent normally falls on the penultimate syllable' as the default for nouns, but adds that Fa d'Ambô stress is not fixed: verbs are final-stressed, heavy (closed/nasal) final syllables attract stress, and a few words are antepenult-stressed, i.e. a weight- and category-conditioned three-syllable window rather than plain fixed penult. This matches Vila 1891 (verbs oxytone; vowel-final nouns penult; consonant-final words oxytone) and the Silveira et al. 2013 transcriptions already. On tone it is consistent with Post (stress, not tone, is the operative category). Note the explicit rule (p. 314, p. 417) is formulated for the reconstructed proto-creole (PGG) and just…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Fa d'Ambô (as for the other three Gulf of Guinea creoles) stress falls within a three-syllable window at the right edge: nouns ending in a light (CV) syllable are stressed on the penult (["pOtO] 'door', ["pÕte] 'bridge'), nouns ending in a heavy syllable (closed/CVN, in FA realized with long or nasal vowel) are stressed on the final ([ku:"sã] 'heart', [bO"nE]), verbs are stressed on the final syllable ([ka"ma] 'burn', [sugu"la] 'hold'), and a small set is antepenult-stressed, in FA often through vowel epenthesis after stress assignment (["pulusu] < *pulsu, ["xobolo] < *kOblO). The author analyses the (proto-)system as right-to-left moraic trochees, weight-sensitive, with word class (noun vs verb) as a lexical conditioning factor and a post-lexical clash-driven stress shift in compounds. On tone (§3.5, p. 262): Barrena 1957 and Segorbe 2007 do not mention tone for Fa d'Ambô and the author's preliminary analysis of Ano Bom recordings 'suggests that accent is a relevant prosodic unit, as in the other languages'; §3.4 (Fa d'Ambô phonology, pp. 233-257) has no accent subsection of its own.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only for the proto-creole/compounds: heads of non-main feet carry secondary stress (e.g. *desu paga [ˌdesu paˈga], *kOta bEga with clash-driven retraction [ˌkOta ˈbEga], p. 320); nothing specific to Fa d'Ambô secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenult items (["pulusu], ["xobolo], ["sabudu] 'sábado') handled by extrametricality/epenthesis; FA ["alma] 'alma' penult where the sisters have ["alima]; some verbs prefinal (["mẼdu] 'temer') and some light-final nouns oxytone ([ku"pi] 'saliva', explained as category change after stress assignment); Edoid- and Bantu-etymon nouns typically final-stressed even with light final syllable ([kũ"du] FA 'tubarão').
new_statements.identity_note: Bandeira 2017 is a reconstruction of the Gulf of Guinea proto-creole (PGG); its Fa d'Ambô data (labelled FA, Ano Bom island = Glottolog fada1250) come from Barrena 1957, Segorbe 2007/2010, Post 1995 and the author's group's own Ano Bom recordings. The explicit weight-sensitive rule is stated for PGG and illustrated with identical Fa d'Ambô reflexes; the direct Fa d'Ambô claim is the three-syllable window with final/penult/antepenult examples.

readall_conflicts: No outright contradiction, but a difference in type: the catalog's existing statement (Post 2013, APiCS) records Fa d'Ambô as penultimate stress ('normally falls on the penultimate syllable'), whereas Bandeira 2017 (pp. 312-314, 417) states that in Fa d'Ambô, as in its sister creoles, stress may fall on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, with penult the default for nouns ending in a light syllable, final stress for verbs and for words ending in a heavy (closed/nasal) syllable, and rare antepenult cases. Post's 'normally' leaves room for exactly these classes, and Vila 1891 and Silveira et al. 2013 (already) show the same verb-final / consonant-final-oxytone pattern, so the sources converge on 'penult default, weight- and word-class-conditioned' rather than strictly fixed penult. All sources agree tone is marginal (Post: a few tonal minimal pairs; Bandeira: earlier grammars do not mention tone, accent is the relevant unit).
